Seminar Title:

Metal Ion-Directed Self-assembly of Guanosine and Structurally Related Purine- and Pterin-Based Molecules into Supramolecular Polymer Hydrogels

Seminar Type:

Department:

Seminar Hall, Chemistry

Date and Time:

Contact:

Bimalendu Adhikari

Abstract:

Supramolecular polymers constructed through reversible non-covalent interactions exhibit unique dynamic properties but often suffer from limited thermal, dilution, and long-term stability, restricting their practical applications. This thesis establishes a metal ion-directed self-assembly strategy for constructing robust supramolecular polymer hydrogels from guanosine and structurally related molecular systems by exploiting the unique coordination chemistry of soft Lewis acid metal ions. Dimercury(I) directs the formation of a previously unexplored octameric guanosine G-quadruplex, in which two G-quartets are covalently linked through an Hg&ndashHg bond. These assemblies undergo supramolecular polymerization to produce highly stable, thermo-reversible, and self-healing hydrogels with superior stability over conventional K⁺-stabilized G-quadruplexes. The study also provides new molecular insights into mercury&ndashguanosine interactions and may contribute to understanding the molecular basis of mercury-induced genotoxicity (Small, 2025). Using inosine as a structurally related analogue of guanosine, Cu(I) directs the formation of the first stable supramolecular inosine I-quadruplexes through metal coordination and Cu⁺&middot&middot&middotCu⁺ metallophilic interactions, producing robust supramolecular polymers with thermoresponsive and redox-reversible properties (manuscript under preparation). Extending this strategy beyond purine systems, Ag(I) directs the self-assembly of folic acid through pterin coordination to generate highly stable supramolecular polymers and hydrogels (Biomacromolecules, 2024). Furthermore, Hofmeister ions regulate the stability and mechanical properties of these supramolecular polymers, where kosmotropic anions reinforce hydrophobic interactions and induce salting-out, whereas chaotropic anions enhance polymer solubility (Biomacromolecules, 2024). Overall, this thesis establishes metal ion-directed self-assembly as a general molecular design strategy for developing robust and stimuli-responsive supramolecular polymer hydrogels from biologically relevant molecular systems. By integrating metal coordination, hydrogen bonding, &pi&ndash&pi stacking, metallophilic interactions, and external ionic regulation, this work advances the fundamental understanding of supramolecular polymerization and provides new molecular design principles for constructing highly stable supramolecular soft materials.
